# 17-expanse — sources

Back-test entry `17-expanse.yaml`: Expanse, job sizes predicted at submit time on shared GPU clusters (YC Spring 2026,
P26). Written 2026-10-22 from public material only, read that day. Quotes are verbatim from the page named. "Author's
choice" marks the smallest plausible choice made where the public material is silent. The launch era is the Launch YC
post of 2026-05-04 and the Launch HN of 2026-06-01 (the founder's gap-11 rule: every figure pinned to the launch era
where one exists; anything later is marked as later and sits under *Status today*).

Main sources (short names used below):
- [LYC] Launch YC: "Expanse - Unlock wasted GPU capacity", 2026-05-04 (created_at in the page data) — https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/QCF-expanse-unlock-wasted-gpu-capacity
- [HN] Launch HN: "Launch HN: Expanse (YC P26) – Unlock Wasted GPU Capacity", 2026-06-01, the founders' post and the thread (27 comments), read whole through the HN Algolia API — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48356312 (https://hn.algolia.com/api/v1/items/48356312)
- [WB] expanse.sh as archived 2026-06-01, the day of the Launch HN — https://web.archive.org/web/20260601142950/https://expanse.sh/
- [YCP] YC company page, read 2026-10-22 — https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/expanse
- [SITE] expanse.sh, read 2026-10-22 — https://expanse.sh

## The eight founder-emulation items

1. **Who.** Researchers and ML engineers who submit jobs to a shared SLURM or Kubernetes GPU cluster.
   [LYC] "Running compute on a cluster means guessing memory, time, and GPUs before you submit."
   [HN] "We also flag failures we think are about to happen and surface line-level optimisations the researcher can apply
   themselves." → `roles[researcher]`, `context.actor`, `actor_plural`.

2. **What (the job).** Get each job to run to the end without wasting the cluster.
   [LYC] "Get it wrong and your job fails mid-run. Over-guess and you pay for compute you never use."
   [HN] "under-requesting kills your job mid-run and you lose days of work. So everyone over-requests by two to three
   times." → `statements.problem`, `context.job`, `interpretations.problem`.

3. **When / where.** At every job submission. [HN] "We scan any workloads about to be submitted through SLURM/K8s
   (plugging into the life cycles of the job so you don't have to change how you submit things)". → `context.circumstance`,
   `occasion: job submission`. Author's choice: the window {5, WORKING_DAYS} (several submissions a working day) and
   Frequency 3 to 5 working days out of 5; Prevalence `p_80_100` ("everyone over-requests").

4. **Which people.** Researchers on SLURM or Kubernetes clusters of 100 or more GPUs, at national HPC centres, AI labs,
   quant funds and drug discovery.
   [HN] "If you run a HPC/GPU cluster (SLURM or K8s, 100+ GPUs), we'd love to have a talk." [LYC] "Know anyone in AI
   infrastructure (managing cloud and/or on-premise data centres), quant finance, drug discovery, or AI research labs?"
   → `context.segment`, `market: US`. Author's choice: US (rule U); the founders are in Edinburgh and the cluster they
   measured is a national-scale HPC site, and their ask names no country.

5. **Who pays.** The cluster's operator, per cluster; a department runs the paid pilot.
   [HN] "We offer a two-week measurement window where we install, ingest, and report recoverable capacity to datacenter
   operators, followed by a paid pilot deployment in one department at a fixed monthly fee, renewing at the same rate
   unless the scope expands." → `persona.decision_maker: {role: operator}`; Buyer and payer tests "The department head"
   (the author's reading of "in one department"), "The security team" listed. Purchase friction's tested item, "A security
   review of an agent on every node", from [HN] "Expanse installs on every node" and the thread's security objection
   ("Any competent enterprise risk team is going to give a hard no to a SaaS application being in the critical path for
   on-prem business critical workloads.") with the founder's reply ("Deployments are air-gapped and run in the customer's
   VPC, on their own hardware."); "Letting it read job scripts and source code" from [HN] "We read the source code, job
   submission script, and the hardware"; the budget line for the department's pilot is the author's. Commitment's step,
   "run a two-week waste measurement on the cluster": [WB] "Two weeks on your cluster. A real wastage number. No
   commitment. If the numbers don't justify a pilot, you walk away with the report." (The same post also offers "a
   section of your cluster for a week"; the two weeks of the pricing paragraph and the site are used.)

6. **Mechanism.** An agent on every node, hooked into the scheduler; a cluster-specific model predicts what each job needs
   at submit time.
   [HN] "Expanse installs on every node and hooks into SLURM (or the K8s scheduler). It ingests live hardware telemetry
   (DCGM, CUPTI, Cgroups, Network/IO monitoring)". [HN] "We predict the GPU VRAM, Utilisation, memory, CPUs and walltime
   the job actually needs, with a confidence interval." [HN] "If a workload fails, we take all the data we collected and
   perform correlations on the stack profiling and the hardware telemetry". [LYC] "All analysis runs on your network."
   → `statements.solution`, `solution_mechanism`. Compatibility: the source code on the cluster beside the script
   (tested; the model reads it), the usual scheduler, Python ([HN] "currently only supported in python - other languages
   coming soon", of the profiler) — the conditions are the author's from these lines. Adoption friction: using the
   suggested sizes instead of padding (tested; [HN] "Our models are trained to over-provision rather than
   under-provision"), applying the code fixes. Relative advantage: [LYC] "Debug failures in seconds, not days"
   (fewer_attempts, the job runs first time) and a shorter queue wait for smaller requests (shorter_time, the author's
   reading of a smaller request fitting sooner); the wording is the author's.

7. **Price and cost.** Per cluster a month, no figure; the cost is the share of the cluster's GPU hours reserved and
   never used.
   [HN] "We're currently onboarding customers as paid pilots. Pricing is determined per-cluster." No figure exists in
   [LYC], [HN], [WB] or [SITE] (no pricing page). The founder's price, AMOUNT_PERIOD **$10,000 to $20,000 per cluster a
   month**, is the operator's reading: for the smallest cluster the founders address (100 GPUs, about 73,000 GPU hours a
   month), [LYC]'s 30% reserved and unused is about 22,000 GPU hours, which at an assumed $2 to $3 a GPU hour (the
   author's assumption; [HN] prices its $8.5M "At on-demand cloud rates for the same hardware" without naming a rate) is
   about $44,000 to $66,000 a month; a fee of a fifth to a third of the waste on the smallest cluster is the author's
   choice. Existing sacrifice: RATE, about 30% to 59% of the cluster's GPU hours per cluster a month, the low from [LYC],
   the high from [HN]'s measured cluster. Ability to pay is read `budget` by the engine (a percent never compares with
   dollars), so the operators answer the registry's budget question.

8. **Occasions.** The stories are scripted from the thread; no respondent is a real person.
   [HN] (a genomics user) "I do genomics work and my jobs tend to be bursty. They may use a lot of CPU initially, but the
   second half of the job is writing results. This takes only one core, but still the max amount of memory." [HN] (an
   HPC user) "I know from snooping on sumbit scripts and node utilization on the HPC that I use at my institution that
   most submissions leave some compute on the table (and many of them are egregiously bad)." [HN] (a student) "It's not
   trivial to estimate a priori the amount of time required for my simulation to complete, so I overestimate."

Cluster operators (COMMERCIAL_B2B link, Part 3 only; no story by rule). Their picks are the author's, shaped by:
- Gregory Lindqvist, Nadia Kowalski, Marco Bianchi → [HN] the measured national cluster and "Datacenters run at roughly 30% to 40% effective utilisation": operators who see the waste and would pay at the founder's band.
- Arjun Mehta → [HN] "large scale compute industries as well, such as quant funds": a quant-fund platform lead who owns the compute budget, sees more waste than the founder's high and decides alone (against the tested department head).
- Beatrix Okoro → [HN] "What you are really left with is the 'small and medium business' clusters that are purpose specific": a small cluster, less waste, a lower rung.
- Thomas Reinholt → [HN] the security objection ("a hard no"); would not pay.

The split (4 of 7 operators at the founder's rung or above; 5 of 6 who give a number at 30% waste or more) is the
author's reading of a thread that agreed on the waste and argued about security and the business. No respondent
carries the name of a commenter, customer or founder.

## Status today

Same idea, five months after launch. [SITE] "Expanse delivers compute certainty. We predict exactly what every job
needs before it runs", still sales-led ("Book a discovery call"), now citing "$8M Monthly wastage uncovered" (a later
figure, not used). [YCP] lists the company as Spring 2026 with the Launch YC text. No public price today ([SITE] has no
pricing page, read 2026-10-22).

## Could not be sourced

- **A price figure.** None at launch or today; the founder's $10,000 to $20,000 per cluster a month is the operator's
  (author's) reading, and the GPU-hour rate behind its arithmetic is an assumption.
- **The waste per cluster as an operator would read it.** The founders' 30% is an industry figure they cite and their
  59% is one national cluster; the operators' value boxes (20% to 60%) are the author's.
- **A buyer title and who has to agree.** [HN] names "datacenter operators" and "one department"; the decider role, the
  department head as the tested role and the security team are the author's reading.
- **A US market.** The founders are in Edinburgh; the US is the author's choice under rule U.
- **A researcher's hour.** No source; `hourly_rate` 60 is a round stand-in, unread by the RATE cost.
- The Compatibility and Adoption friction conditions, the Purchase friction items but the security review, and every
  pick are the author's.

founder.order_why: It runs from naming and market, to the context (who, when, how far back), to the problem's belief and story, then to interview setup, which is how I'd explain Expanse to someone new.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 3 and 5 carry the same heading ('Before we test anything, let's define exactly where this idea applies.') with the look-back window between them, so it reads as the context being asked for twice.
founder.missing: The belief questions (8 and 9) only ask about a job failing on a memory guess. My core problem is the other side: everyone over-requests by two to three times and the reserved GPUs sit idle (59% wasted on the cluster we measured). There was no question about how many researchers padded their request, or by how much, and failure is only half of what I believe is true.

PRIMARY.order_why: Screen 4 jumps to a broad 'what would you most like made easier' question between the memory-failure questions and screen 5, which goes back to how guessing memory, time and GPUs went on my last submission, so 5 would fit better right after 3.
PRIMARY.asked_twice: Screens 2 and 3: whether a job failed on a memory guess in the last 5 days, and then on how many of those days, which already covers the yes/no.
PRIMARY.missing: Jobs killed for running past the requested wall time rather than memory, and how much work was lost when a job died mid-run (days of a fine-tuning run, whether I had checkpoints). Also the other side: over-requesting to be safe and then waiting longer in the queue or holding GPUs I didn't use.

screens.why7: Partition choice sits at the submit moment, but moving data and getting software working happen before or after submission rather than when the job is being sized, so two rivals drift outside the moment the circumstance names.
screens.instead: Keep the question; as rivals: Choosing which partition or queue to submit to; Checking the group's GPU-hour allocation before submitting; Setting how often the job checkpoints.

screens.why1: Right after I named the other things that are hard at submit time, checking the list that strangers will hear is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: Partition, queue and GPU-hour allocation are plain cluster words to me, but the own row reads 'Guessing the memory to request yours', with a stray 'yours' that looks like the UI label leaking into the text, so it needs a second read.
screens.why3: Every row is something a researcher on a shared SLURM or K8s cluster does themselves around submitting a job: sizing it, picking a partition, staging data, getting software to build, and watching the group's allocation.
screens.why4: The rivals are distinct and in my trade's words, but the own row is garbled by the trailing 'yours', and data staging and software setup sit a little outside the moment a job is ready to submit.
screens.why5: My problem is guessing memory, GPUs and walltime so the job neither dies mid-run nor sits on two to three times what it uses; 'Guessing the memory to request' keeps memory only and loses the GPUs, the walltime and the failure-or-waste stake.
screens.why7: The shape holds: own row first, four rivals, five in all, one bar of 'one of their two'. The own row bends the card's rule, though: it is narrowed to one part (memory) and restates the circumstance's 'have to be guessed' rather than naming the hurt, while the rivals stay on the one measure, so the belief can still be supported or refuted.

screens.why1: Checking the difficulty list right after naming the other hard things at submit time is the obvious next step before strangers hear it.
screens.why2: Partition, queue, memory request and getting the job's software to load are everyday words to anyone submitting to SLURM or Kubernetes.
screens.why3: Every row is something a researcher does at submission on their own cluster, answerable from last week's jobs.
screens.why4: The rivals are distinct and real, but moving data on and off the cluster sits a little outside the moment of submitting, and the own row covers memory alone while GPUs and run time drop out.
screens.why5: My problem is sizing the whole job (memory, GPUs and walltime) so it neither fails nor wastes the cluster, and 'Guessing the memory to request' narrows it to one part and leans on the circumstance's own word 'guessed'.
screens.why7: The shape holds (own row first and locked, three rivals, so a stranger can fill both picks without it, and the belief can go either way), but the own row bends A3 and the 'never narrowed to one part' rule by restating the circumstance's guess and keeping only memory.

screens.why1: After belief, frequency and what else is hard, asking how researchers cope today is the obvious next step before Keel tests whether that way falls short.
screens.why2: 'How do they deal with it today?' with the hint about the one step and what they do it with is plain to me, and my answer stays in the cluster's own words: memory, GPUs, run time, submit, mid-run.
screens.why3: Over-requesting two to three times so a job doesn't die mid-run is exactly what I've watched researchers do and what our measurements show, so I answer from what I know.
screens.why4: The two boxes take my act and my rungs cleanly, and 'I'm not sure' is the right founder-side escape, leaving the dimension out.
screens.why5: Both boxes hold my words verbatim: the guess-and-pad act and my three rungs on idle reservation, and nothing about Expanse leaks into them.
screens.why7: The first box names the act and its means within 25 words; the second gives three rungs of 9 words or fewer, all on one measure (how much of the reservation sat idle) and best to worst; the first rung, 'Ran first time, sized about right', is today's way working, so the line can sit under it and Keel can add the worse rungs to five.

screens.why1: Right after I said how researchers deal with it today, checking the five outcomes of that habit is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: 'Ran', 'holding twice what it used', 'resubmitted' are exactly how anyone on a SLURM cluster talks about a job.
screens.why3: Every researcher knows whether their last job ran, died partway, or sat on far more memory and GPUs than it touched.
screens.why4: The ladder switches axes partway (rungs 1-3 grade how much was over-held, 4-5 grade whether it finished), and someone who held about 1.5x falls between 'about right' and 'about twice'.
screens.why5: These are my rungs as I typed them, and the belief reads guessing memory, time and GPUs back in my words.
screens.why7: Shape, working first rung, line, balance and escape all hold, but 'Failed partway and had to be resubmitted' sits under three rungs of idle reservation, the off-measure case the card itself names, so the one-measure rule is bent.
screens.instead: Think of the last job you submitted. How did sizing it go? Ran first time, sized about right · Ran, holding about twice what it used · Ran, holding three times or more what it used · Ran only after a resubmit · Never ran to the end · I can't recall

screens.why1: Choosing who asks the questions belongs right before the study goes out, after the problem rows are checked.
screens.why2: The question and hint are plain, and AI interviewer, video, text message are clear to an infra founder.
screens.why3: Picking the interviewer is my own call as the founder sending the study.
screens.why4: The preselected face is fine, but nothing says whether researchers can opt out of video, and an SMS link is odd for researchers who live in email and Slack.
screens.why5: Nothing here changes what I typed, and no product or role wording leaks to respondents.
screens.instead: Who should ask your questions? (Keel's AI interviewer on video, with every question also on screen to read and tap; link sent by text or email)

screens.why1: After choosing who asks the questions, picking how the researchers answer is the obvious next step before sending.
screens.why2: Video interviewer, read and tap, or let them choose are plain to any ML engineer or researcher on first read.
screens.why3: As the founder I know my researchers sit at a terminal between submits and would rather tap through than talk to a video, so I can answer this from what I know.
screens.why4: The three options cover the two formats and the mix, are distinct, and none is missing or odd; no escape chip is needed for a format choice.
screens.why5: It keeps my actor wording (researchers and ML engineers) and leaks nothing of Expanse's product into the choice.

screens.why1: After choosing how researchers answer, deciding who gets the link is the natural last step before sending, and it asks nothing already answered.
screens.why2: Plain words throughout; 'Contacts page' is Keel's own screen and reads clearly enough in context, and 'signs in with Google' is plain to anyone on a cluster.
screens.why3: I know exactly who I'd reach: researchers on clusters I've talked to by name, so it's answerable from what I do.
screens.why4: Three distinct routes (named people, a Keel-found list, an open link posted in a group like a cluster Slack or mailing list) cover the real ways I'd reach researchers, with no overlap and no escape needed.
screens.why5: Nothing of my product or roles is touched here; it's a delivery choice and my pick, people I know by name, is kept.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits right beside the number that decides it, 'Frequency: 4 counted', and the method line says the worst card sets the verdict, so I can see why the stage did not get called even though Prevalence held.
screens.why_b2: Prevalence's '6 of 7 said yes · bar 6 of 7 · at the bar' reads at once, but the kicker's '4 TO 7 COUNTED' made me look twice before I worked out it means the cards counted different numbers of my seven people.
screens.why_b3: The dimension names are mine, but the belief lines narrow my problem to 'a job fail on a memory guess', and my claim was that people pad two to three times so jobs mostly run while the GPUs sit idle; Importance still names 'Guessing the memory to request' rather than sizing a job to neither fail nor waste GPUs.
screens.why_b4: Nothing on the page says what this means for Expanse or what to do; the only hint is '5 needed to call it' on each card, and the page never says to get more researchers answering or which answers would settle Frequency, Importance and Current solution.
screens.why_b5: The number of people stays visible on every line, the low counts are named as too few to call, and the one held belief is marked 'at the bar' with 6 of 7 rather than called strong.
screens.instead: Too few to call: only 4 of my 7 researchers could be counted on how often, how much it matters and what they do now (5 needed); 6 of 7 did hit a sizing failure this week, so get at least a few more researchers through the study before reading the rest, and test the padding-and-idle-GPUs belief, not just jobs dying on memory.

screens.why_b1: 'Holding up' sits right beside '6 of 7 said yes · bar 6 of 7 · at the bar', so I know it held and by exactly how much: one more No and it would not have.
screens.why_b2: The strip shows 6 for and 1 against out of 7, with the marker at 6 labelled as my 'at least 8 in 10', so what is counted, over how many and where my bar sits are plain at first look.
screens.why_b3: Prevalence and 'at least 8 in 10' are mine, but the people lost my 'on SLURM or Kubernetes clusters of 100 or more GPUs', and the gate's '— the most recent time it happened' tacked onto a yes/no question reads as a leftover from another card.
screens.why_b4: 'How often, and whether it matters, are the next two cards' points me onward, but it never says what a failed memory guess in 6 of 7 means for selling submit-time sizing, such as leading with failures as well as waste.
screens.why_b5: It keeps n=7 in view, calls it 'a small group: a lean, not a call', and limits the claim to 'Common among these 7, at your bar exactly' instead of calling it strong.
screens.instead: At least 8 in 10 researchers on SLURM or Kubernetes clusters of 100+ GPUs had a job fail on a memory guess -- holding, 6 of 7 at your bar of 6, a lean from 7 people; failures are common enough to lead the pitch with, check Frequency next.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits right beside the deciding numbers, '4 counted · 5 needed to call it', and the So line ties the two together.
screens.why_b2: The middle answer of 4 and the strip's '4 of 5 (at least 2 in 3)' are plain, but it takes a second look to work out the legend's 'what you said · at what you said · short of it' and why the axis has a 0 tick when nobody could answer 0.
screens.why_b3: The window and my 3 to 5 working days are mine, but 'have a job fail on a memory guess' narrows my problem, which is guessing memory, GPUs and run time and over-requesting, to failures alone; and 'the most recent time it happened' tacked onto a count question is not how I asked it.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' is generic; it does not tell me that one more counted answer would decide it, or that all four so far sit inside my range.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible (6 answered, 4 counted, why two were not counted) and the small group is called 'a lean, not a call', so nothing claims more than four people can carry.
screens.instead: Too few to call: all 4 counted researchers sit inside your 3 to 5 working days (middle answer 4), so it leans your way; one more counted answer decides it, and the question should ask about guessing a job's memory, GPUs and run time, not only failures.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits right beside its number, '4 counted · 5 needed to call it', and the two agree.
screens.why_b2: The bars count picks (8) while the strip counts people. The bar reads '4 of 5', which sits right next to '4 counted', so I had to look twice to see that 3 of 4 put my problem in their two and that 4 is the bar, not the count.
screens.why_b3: My problem is guessing memory, GPUs and run time before submitting, but the belief and the chart narrow it to 'Guessing the memory to request'. I recognise it, but it is one part of my problem, not the whole.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' is generic: it doesn't say that one more counted answer decides it, or that the lean so far is 3 for and 1 against.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible and the small group is named 'a lean, not a call'; nothing claims more than four counted answers can carry.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits right beside its deciding number, '4 counted · 5 needed to call it', and the two agree.
screens.why_b2: The rungs with their counts and the line are plain, but the strip's 'your bar · 4 of 5' with a ghost cell, against 4 people counted, took me a second look to read as 'what it would take at the floor of 5'.

screens.why_b1: The status word 'Too few to call' sits directly above '4 counted · 5 needed to call it', so I know there is no verdict yet and which number decides that.
screens.why_b3: Importance is my dimension, but the belief names 'Guessing the memory to request', not the row I checked ('Sizing a job to neither fail nor waste GPUs'); I recognise it but it isn't my wording.
screens.why_b4: Nothing tells me what to do: not that I need one more researcher's answer to call it, and not whether data movement and software loading should become rows I test.

screens.why1: As the first screen it obviously checks whether I'm the right person: someone who submits jobs to a big shared GPU cluster.
screens.why2: Run jobs, cluster and GPUs are my everyday words, and I can answer it the moment I hear it.
screens.why3: I know which cluster I submit to and roughly how many GPUs it has, so I can answer from my own work.
screens.why4: Yes or no covers it, and the gate correctly has no escape.
screens.why5: Nothing leaks, but the founder's segment says SLURM or Kubernetes and a last-five-working-days window, and both are dropped, so someone with an old account or a non-shared box could slip through.
screens.why6: "I'll read 2 options. Yes; or No." is a stiff wrapper for a yes-or-no gate, where the amended screener form is just the stem then "Yes or no."
screens.instead: In the last week, did you submit a job to a shared SLURM or Kubernetes cluster with 100 or more GPUs? Yes or no.

screens.why1: Right after confirming I run jobs on a 100+ GPU cluster, asking whether a job died in the last week is the obvious next question.
screens.why2: I know exactly what's meant, but nobody says 'fail on a memory guess'; I'd say a job got OOM-killed or ran out of memory because I under-requested, so it takes a second read.
screens.why3: Whether one of my jobs got killed for memory this week is something I know cold from the logs and the lost hours.
screens.why4: Yes or No is complete and distinct for a gate, and the chips belong to the story box after a Yes, not to this answer.
screens.why5: The founder's problem is under-requesting killing a job mid-run, which covers wall time and GPUs too, but the gate narrows it to memory only, so someone whose job hit its time limit truthfully says No.
screens.why6: It's short and one question, and 'Yes or no' is easy to hold when heard once.
screens.why7: It's a two-answer gate on the costly event, not the routine of guessing resources, so a researcher whose jobs all finished says No and one who got OOM-killed says Yes, with no escape on the gate itself.
screens.instead: In the last 5 working days, did you have a job killed mid-run because you asked for too little memory or time? Yes · No

screens.why1: Right after I said yes to having a job fail on memory in the last week, asking how many of those days it happened is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: I'd say a job got OOM-killed or ran out of memory, not that it 'failed on a memory guess', so I'd pause a second to map that phrase onto an OOM kill.
screens.why3: I know which days this week my jobs got OOM-killed, because I'm the one who resubmitted them.
screens.why4: One button per working day from 1 to 5, no zero since I already said yes, and 'I can't recall' kept apart: complete and distinct.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's job-fails-on-a-guessed-number idea without leaking any product or the founder's own terms beyond the slightly bookish 'memory guess'.
screens.why6: Heard once it's one short question, then 'a number from 1 to 5' and one escape, which is easy to answer aloud.
screens.why7: It counts days, not times, says the unit once in the window phrase, offers 1 to 5 in order with 5 as the window's count, and has the one cant_recall escape apart, so the founder's low can split the buttons.
screens.instead: On how many of the last 5 working days did you have a job killed for running out of memory? 1 · 2 · 3 · 4 · 5 · I can't recall

screens.why1: Right after asking how often a memory guess killed my job, it makes sense to ask how that pain ranks against the other things that slow my runs down.
screens.why2: Partition, queue, software loading, memory request and moving data on and off are all words I use every day on SLURM, so I can answer on first read.
screens.why3: These are four things I deal with myself every time I submit, and I know which one costs me the most days.
screens.why4: Four distinct, parallel tasks in my own words, with 'None of these' as a fitting way out; 'partition or queue' is one choice named for both SLURM and Kubernetes, not two things.
screens.why5: 'Guessing the memory to request' keeps the memory guess that kills my runs, and nothing about a product or the founder's plans shows through.
screens.why6: It is one short question with four short options spoken as a list I can hold, and one escape said last.
screens.why7: The own row is present and not first, three rivals are each a separate difficulty I meet at submit time, the pick-one hint matches the first ask, and 'None of these' is there and counts against, so the belief can be supported or refuted.

screens.why1: Right after I said what I'd most like made easier, asking how my last submission's sizing actually went is the obvious next thing to ask.
screens.why2: Every word is mine, but memory, time and GPUs are three guesses in one stem, and one of them can be fine while another is badly off, so I'd have to reread to know which one I'm grading.
screens.why3: I know exactly how my last submission went, whether it OOM'd or sat holding far more than it used.
screens.why4: Failed partway and had to be resubmitted overlaps with never ran to the end, since a job that failed partway also never ran to the end, and the escape I can't recall fits because I size my own jobs.
screens.why5: Nothing of a product or the founder's terms reaches me; it is just my own job sizing in my own words.
screens.why6: It hears fine as five options, but the stem's three-item list and ran, holding three times or more what it used are a mouthful to hold on one hearing.
screens.why7: There is a working first rung, the escape is right, and below-line answers could support or refute the belief, but the last two rungs switch from how much was held idle to whether the job finished, which is the card's own named stand-in under rungs of idle reservation.
screens.instead: Think of your last job submission. How close was what you asked for to what it used? Sized about right; about twice what it used; three to five times what it used; over five times what it used; asked too little and it died. Or say you can't recall.
